title: US Navy Opens Formal Evaluation of Japanese, Korean and Turkish Frigate Designs as DARPA Launches Next-Gen Hypersonic Cruise Missile Program
subhead: Washington moves to buy allied-built warships — Japan's Mogami, South Korea's Chungnam and Turkey's Istanbul-class — to rebuild its surface fleet after the Constellation collapse, while DARPA kicks off a production-focused scramjet cruise missile demonstrator and the Navy advances its nuclear SLCM-N fire control.

sections.heading: US Navy Formally Evaluates Three Foreign Frigate Designs
sections.body:
On September 1, the U.S. Navy began formal evaluation of Japan's Mogami-class, South Korea's Chungnam-class and Turkey's Istanbul-class frigates as candidates to restore conventional surface capacity after the truncation of the domestic Constellation-class program, according to USNI News and Army Recognition. The foreign-procurement framework, set under an August 13 acquisition framework, allocates $1.85 billion in FY2027 funds to buy up to two overseas-built lead ships before transferring construction to U.S. yards from hull 3 onward. An initial assessment deadline is set for November 12.

The three designs differ sharply: Japan's Mogami-class displaces roughly 5,500 tons with a low-manning architecture of about 90 sailors; South Korea's Chungnam-class (FFX Batch III) runs about 4,300 tons and is already built across three yards; Turkey's Istanbul-class is the smallest at roughly 3,100 tons but carries a dense battery of 16 Atmaca anti-ship missiles and 16 MiDLAS VLS cells.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a direct test of whether the U.S. Navy can buy a ship already in serial production and localize it without repeating the Constellation failure — where a FREMM-derived design ballooned past 7,800 tons and was cut to two hulls. Turkey has seven Istanbul-class frigates in build across three private yards, South Korea can surge to 3-4 hulls a year, and Japan is already running a two-ship-a-year rhythm.

sections.heading: DARPA Launches Next-Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile With Production Focus
sections.body:
On September 2, DARPA's Tactical Technology Office published a Special Notice announcing an Industry Day for the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile (NGHCM) program, scheduled for September 22 in Arlington, Virginia, Army Recognition reports. The program aims to design, build and flight-test an air-breathing scramjet demonstrator with gains in range, cruise speed and altitude.

The defining feature is that DARPA is embedding Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DFMA) requirements from project inception — a direct response to a July 2026 Government Accountability Office assessment finding the Common Hypersonic/Conventional Prompt Strike and Dark Eagle production effort could build only six to seven rounds annually versus the 12 per year needed for stability, with Conventional Prompt Strike rounds estimated at $63-71 million each. NGHCM differs structurally from the boost-glide Dark Eagle: a booster accelerates the missile before a scramjet sustains hypersonic cruise using atmospheric oxygen.
sections.whyItMatters: The U.S. hypersonic bottleneck is now openly acknowledged to be manufacturing, not flight technology. By tying DFMA into early engineering trades, DARPA is trying to prevent a design that flies but cannot be produced affordably at wartime rates — with Air Force HACM procurement of $403.9 million requested in FY2027 showing the near-term track.

sections.heading: GE Lands $2.87B F414 Sustainment Deal and Mach 5 Hypersonic Test Vehicle Contract
sections.body:
The U.S. Navy awarded General Electric a logistics contract worth up to $2.87 billion on September 1 to sustain F414-GE-400 engines powering the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler fleets through August 2031, Army Recognition reports. The five-year ceiling, under contract N00383-26-D-UA01, covers 17 engine component families including hot-section parts, with an initial delivery order of $198.2 million accompanying the award. Work is split between Lynn, Massachusetts (90%) and Jacksonville, Florida (10%).

Separately, GE Aerospace won a Defense Innovation Unit contract to advance the HyCAT (Hypersonic and High-Cadence Airborne Testing Capabilities) program, developing Derecho, an air-launched Mach 5 hypersonic test vehicle, Breaking Defense and aviationnews.eu report. The DIU work moves the liquid-fueled testbed into full integration and qualification testing.
sections.whyItMatters: The F414 deal is a sustainment hedge: Boeing's Super Hornet line is closing (final 17 Block IIIs ordered in March 2024), yet the Navy will keep the F/A-18 and Growler flying for years amid F/A-XX schedule pressure. The separate HyCAT award pairs the industrial sustainment story with the hypersonic testing bottleneck DARPA is also attacking.

sections.heading: Navy Pushes SLCM-N Nuclear Cruise Missile With New Fire Control Award
sections.body:
On September 3, the U.S. Department of War disclosed a $194.1 million contract modification to General Dynamics Mission Systems for engineering of the SLCM-N fire control subsystem, the nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile program, Army Recognition reports. The cost-plus-fixed-fee modification (PZ0002) runs through September 2028, with about 75% of work in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. Roughly $135.3 million in FY2025 RDT&E funds were obligated at award.

The program passed its Milestone A decision in December 2025 and targets limited operational capability by fiscal 2032 and initial operational capability by fiscal 2034. The FY2026 Mandatory Funding Allocation Plan provides $2 billion for the SLCM-N effort, including $793.6 million in Navy RDT&E. The award is a revival of a capability category the U.S. retired in 2013 with the nuclear Tomahawk (TLAM-N), this time for integration aboard Virginia-class attack submarines with the Virginia Payload Module.
sections.whyItMatters: SLCM-N is being built as a regional nuclear deterrent from attack submarines — deliberately distinct from the strategic SSBN force. The fire control award shows the program shifting from concept toward integrated submarine weapon-system engineering, adding a non-ballistic, covert-dispersed sea-based nuclear option.

sections.heading: Russia Offers 'Bizon' Counter-Drone System to Egypt
sections.body:
Russia's state defense conglomerate Rostec is offering the export TKB-1167 'Bizon' counter-drone system to Egypt, The Defense Post reports (September 4). The Bizon, developed by Rostec's High-Precision Systems arm, is the export version of the Russian army's Zubr short-range air defense system. It autonomously detects and tracks small, low-flying targets and engages them with 7.62 mm PKT machine guns, with the final engagement decision reserved for a human operator.

The offer follows Cairo's report of an unprecedented drone strike on its Damietta Port in July, during the Iran-Israel-US conflict. According to Rostec's industrial director for armaments, Bekhan Ozdoev, the Bizon is 'already on combat duty and successfully engaging real targets.'
sections.whyItMatters: The offer reflects a broader export push for war-tested counter-drone technology. Egypt is a major Russian arms customer, and the pitch positions Moscow's battle-proven C-UAS kit against a regional drone-threat market — one Turkish and other suppliers are also actively contesting.

sections.heading: Pentagon Faces Further Leadership Turmoil as Feinberg Successor Candidates Reviewed
sections.body: The White House has reviewed candidates to potentially replace Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg, three people familiar with the discussions told Reuters (September 5), signaling more leadership change for a Pentagon already facing unusually high staff turnover. The development follows the resignation of the Army Secretary and other departures in recent weeks that have reshaped the department's top civilian ranks.
sections.whyItMatters: After successive departures (including the Army Secretary earlier this week), the prospect of replacing the No. 2 civilian adds fresh uncertainty over Pentagon procurement priorities and program direction at a moment of major acquisition decisions — from foreign frigate evaluation to hypersonic and nuclear modernization.

bottomLine: The defining story of the past week is that the U.S. acquisition system is now openly borrowing foreign industrial capacity to close capability gaps it can no longer close alone: formal evaluation of Japanese, Korean and Turkish frigate designs to rebuild the surface fleet, a production-first DARPA hypersonic demonstrator, and a $2.87B GE sustainment deal to keep the F/A-18 line flying through the F/A-XX gap. Alongside these, the Navy deepened the SLCM-N nuclear cruise missile effort and Russia pushed its Bizon counter-drone system into the Middle East. The common thread is that the world's largest defense buyer is managing scarcity — of hulls, high-end munitions and production throughput — while nuclear and hypersonic programs advance, all under a Pentagon leadership still in flux.
sources: USNI News, Army Recognition, Breaking Defense, aviationnews.eu, The Defense Post, Reuters, GAO
